claims.text: Local element-specific chemical segregation at nanoscale defect sites lowers the effective surface melting temperature of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
This segregation initiates partial premelting before bulk melting.
Segregation-driven premelting governs overall melting behavior and its dependence on composition.
The investigated particles are 5–20 nm Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles synthesized as a room-temperature single-phase solid solution.
Time-resolved in situ TEM with EDS can be used to monitor element-specific migration and structural changes through the premelting regime.
Heating should proceed from ambient temperature to above the equiatomic alloy's bulk melting point at 1–10 K/s.
A sufficiently high quenching rate will preserve observed phase separation or morphological changes.
Elemental segregation, short-range ordering, and defects concentrate in surface and near-surface regions.
These surface features alter local melting points and direct the onset of premelting.
Cu may segregate to the surface while Cr stabilizes internal regions of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Element-specific atomic diffusion lowers local surface melting temperatures and accelerates partial melt formation.
Localized molten patches act as nucleation sites for complete dissolution of the remaining solid as temperature rises.
Rapid quenching after melting can preserve a metastable or stable single-phase solid solution.
Relative to pure Ni or binary Ni–Cu nanoparticles, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will begin partial premelting at a lower temperature, below the bulk alloy melting point.
Premelting will be observable as localized liquid islands.
EDS will show transient surface enrichment in lower-melting elements followed by compositional homogenization in the fully molten state.
Comparable pure Ni or Ni–Cu nanoparticles exhibit a relatively sharp melting transition with less premelting or elemental segregation.
The segregation-driven mechanism applies to multicomponent nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in diameter and within tens of degrees of the bulk melting temperature.
The mechanism may fail for significantly larger particles or compositions with stronger solubility constraints.
Uniform melting without detectable surface segregation or early local melting would invalidate the proposed segregation-based mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that rapid quenching should preserve observed phase separation, whereas the mechanism states that rapid quenching can preserve a single-phase solid solution. These are different and potentially incompatible expected quenched states unless conditional criteria are specified.
